edits.old: Four students record the same temperature: 36.8°, 36.08°, 36.80°, and 36.089°. Arrange them in increasing order and state which two are equal.
edits.new: Four students read the same thermometer and write down: 36.8°, 36.08°, 36.80°, and 36.089°. Arrange the readings in increasing order and state which two are equal.

edits.old: Compare left to right. All have 36 as the whole-number part. Tenths: 36.08_ has 0 (smallest), the others have 8. Among those with tenths digit 8: hundredths of 36.8 = 36.80 = 0 (trailing zero), 36.089 has 0, 36.80 has 0 — look further: 36.089 has thousandths digit 9 > 0. So 36.80 = 36.8 (trailing zero does not change value). Order: 36.08 < 36.089 < 36.8 = 36.80. The two equal readings are 36.8 and 36.80.
edits.new: Compare left to right. All have 36 as the whole-number part. Tenths: 36.08 and 36.089 have tenths digit 0; 36.8 and 36.80 have tenths digit 8, so both of the first pair are smaller. Between 36.08 and 36.089: they agree up to the hundredths digit, and 36.089 carries a thousandths digit 9 against 0, so 36.08 < 36.089. Finally 36.80 = 36.8 — a trailing zero does not change the value. Order: 36.08 < 36.089 < 36.8 = 36.80. The two equal readings are 36.8 and 36.80.

textbook_items_in_class.description: Measure the lengths of a pen, sharpener, and an object of the student's choice using a scale; record the measurements in centimetres using tenth notation as modelled in the section.

time_bands.activity: Hold up two visually similar objects (a pen and a pencil) and invite students to say which is longer. Guide a brief discussion about how ordinary whole-centimetre readings fail to distinguish lengths that differ by a small fraction. Introduce Sonu's mother's screw problem from section 3.1 to crystallise why subdividing a centimetre is necessary.

Distribute rulers. Students place their pen and sharpener on the millimetre-ruled scale and attempt to record lengths in whole centimetres, noticing the gap. Teacher models reading a length such as 2 7/10 cm by counting tenths of a centimetre, writing the mixed-number notation on the board and naming each part.

Figure it Out, section 3.1 p.47 ("Measure the lengths of a pen, sharpener, and an object....") — students measure three objects, record each length in the form 'whole number and tenths' notation, and share readings aloud with a partner to check for consistency.

Whole-class close: students name one situation from their own life where a whole-unit measurement would be insufficient, and explain which smaller unit they would want. Teacher collects two or three examples to anchor the language of 'tenths of a centimetre'.

periods.teacher_notes: Build the intuition that whole centimetres are too coarse before any notation is introduced — the cognitive need for smaller units must feel genuine. A common early error is reading the tenths tick as a new whole unit; confirm that ten such ticks span exactly one centimetre. No worked examples are formally defined in this section, so class discussion and measurement drive the entire unit.
materials: Pens and sharpeners of similar length

textbook_items_in_class.description: Write lengths of objects (USB cable, and others shown in diagrams) in two ways — as a mixed number and as an improper tenth fraction — and read them aloud.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.49
textbook_items_in_class.description: Arrange eight lengths in increasing order: (a) 9/10; (b) 1 7/10; (c) 130/10; (d) 13 1/10; (e) 10 5/10; (f) 7 6/10; (g) 6 7/10; (h) 4/10.

homework.description: Arrange four lengths in increasing order: 4 1/10, 4/10, 41/10, 41 1/10.

time_bands.activity: Draw the pencil-length diagram from section 3.2 on the board. Walk through how 34 one-tenths equal three full units plus four tenths, writing the mixed-number notation (3 4/10 units). Students echo-read the notation and state aloud: 'three units and four tenths'.

Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.49 ("Write lengths of objects…in two ways….") — students write each diagram length as both a mixed number and an improper tenth fraction, then read each aloud to a partner. Teacher circulates and checks that students distinguish the whole-unit count from the tenth count.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.49 ("Arrange eight lengths in increasing order….") — students convert each length to a common improper-tenth form, line them up on a number-strip sketch, and write the ordered list. Two volunteers share their orderings and explain any disagreements.
Class debrief: teacher highlights how converting to a single unit of tenths makes ordering straightforward. Homework item from section 3.2 p.50 is set.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the denominator 10 with the number of whole units; pairing the mixed-number and improper-fraction forms in the same exercise exposes this directly. Stress that 34/10 and 3 4/10 name identical lengths by pointing back to the pencil diagram. Watch for students who write the improper fraction by simply appending the tenth digit rather than multiplying whole units by 10.
materials: Squared or plain paper for number strips

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the total length of a honeybee given head = 2 3/10 units, thorax = 5 4/10 units, abdomen = 7 5/10 units.
Find the length of Shylaja's middle finger given total hand length 12 4/10 units and palm length 6 7/10 units; discuss two methods shown and try computing by converting to tenths.
Find the difference in lengths between a Celestial Pearl Danio (2 4/10 cm) and a Philippine Goby (9/10 cm); compare to finger size.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.52
textbook_items_in_class.description: Observe six sequences of tenth-fractions, identify the change after each term, and extend each pattern by four more terms: (a) 4, 4 3/10, 4 6/10, …; (b) 8 2/10, 8 7/10, 9 2/10, …; (c) 7 6/10, 8 7/10, …; (d) 5 7/10, 5 3/10, …; (e) 13 5/10, 13, 12 5/10, …; (f) 11 5/10, 10 4/10, 9 3/10, …

time_bands.activity: Revisit the two addition methods from section 3.2 — 'units and tenths separately' and 'convert all to tenths' — using the arm-length example (2 7/10 + 3 6/10 = 6 3/10) on the board. Students state each step aloud before moving to independent work.

Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.51 ("Find the total length of a honeybee….") and Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.51 ("Find the length of Shylaja's middle finger….") — students solve both items, applying both methods and comparing results. Teacher emphasises the regrouping step when tenths exceed 9.

Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.52 ("Find the difference in lengths….") — students compute the fish-length subtraction, then Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.52 ("Observe six sequences….") in pairs: identify the constant step in each sequence and write four more terms.

Gallery share: pairs present one sequence each, stating the constant addend or subtrahend as a tenth fraction. Class confirms each term by a quick mental check. Teacher closes by noting that the pattern-spotting skill in sequences will recur when decimals replace tenth-fraction notation.

periods.teacher_notes: The subtraction with regrouping (12 4/10 – 6 7/10) trips many students who try to subtract tenths before borrowing a whole unit; model the regrouping explicitly if pairs stall. Observe whether students use both methods or only convert to tenths — encouraging the 'units and tenths' method builds the column-addition intuition needed for section 3.7. Sequences that decrease across a whole-unit boundary (e.g., 13 5/10, 13, 12 5/10) are a common stumbling point.

textbook_items_in_class.description: How many one-hundredths make one-tenth? Can the folded-paper length also be stated as 4 units and 45 one-hundredths? Explain.
Fill the empty boxes in the ruler diagram: given markings at 0, 1/10, 1/100, 2/10, 20/100, 1, 99/100, 130/100, 3/10, 2, identify the missing decimal lengths at each marked position.
For lengths shown in the diagrams, write each measurement in decimal fraction form and read the measurement aloud in words (sample answers: 5 37/100 and 15 3/100 shown in the teacher answer key).

time_bands.activity: Pose the folded-paper problem from section 3.3: a strip of length 8 9/10 units is folded in half — what is the half-length? Students attempt the calculation and quickly discover that tenths alone cannot express the answer. Teacher draws the strip diagram showing each tenth subdivided into 10 parts, establishing that one unit contains 100 one-hundredths.

Math Talk, section 3.3 p.53 ("How many one-hundredths make one-tenth?….") — small groups discuss and then report: 10 hundredths = 1 tenth, and the folded length 4 5/10 45/100 equals 4 units and 45 hundredths. Teacher confirms using the wire diagram (1 1/10 4/100 = 1 14/100 = 114/100) to show multiple representations.

Figure it Out, section 3.3 p.54 ("Fill the empty boxes in the ruler diagram….") and Figure it Out, section 3.3 p.54 ("Write each measurement in decimal fraction form….") — students complete both items individually and read answers aloud in words to confirm they distinguish tenths from hundredths.

Class consolidation: teacher writes three equivalent representations of the same length on the board (mixed tenths-and-hundredths, combined hundredths, improper hundredths) and students vote on which two are equal, then justify. This cements the equivalence scaffold.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently think that 3/10 and 3/100 are close in value because the numerators match; the ruler diagram physically shows how much smaller one hundredth is compared to one tenth. Watch for students who confuse the position of the hundredths digit with the tenths digit when writing combined forms. The wire-diagram representation (1 1/10 4/100 = 1 14/100) from the section prose is the most effective counter to this confusion.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.55
textbook_items_in_class.description: In seven groups (a)–(g), identify the longest and shortest length from the given set of tenths and hundredths values, and mark each length on the scale: (a) 3/10, 3/100, 33/100; (b) 3 1/10, 30/10, 1 3/10; (c) 45/100, 54/100, 5/10, 4/10; (d) 3 6/10, 3 6/100, 3 6/10 6/100; (e) 8 2/100, 9/100, 1 8/100; (f) 7 3/10 5/100, 7 5/10, 7 41/100; (g) 65/10 15/100, 5 87/100, 5 7/100.
Solve by converting to hundredths: find the difference 25 9/10 – 6 4/10 7/100; then find 15 3/10 4/100 – 2 6/10 8/100 and observe structural similarity with whole-number column subtraction 653 – 268.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.58

time_bands.activity: Teacher works through the column-wise place value decomposition method for addition of tenths-and-hundredths on the board, using the two parallel approaches (column decomposition and convert-to-hundredths) side by side. Students observe the structural parallel with whole-number column addition.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.55 ("Identify the longest and shortest length….") — students work items (a)–(d) individually, converting each group to common hundredths and marking positions on a sketch scale. Pairs compare and reconcile any differences in items (e)–(g).

Math Talk, section 3.3 p.57 ("Solve by converting to hundredths: find the difference….") — teacher-led discussion of the two subtractions with the class, writing the column form alongside the conversion form and explicitly aligning the whole-number subtraction 653 – 268 next to 15 3/10 4/100 – 2 6/10 8/100 to highlight structural similarity.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.58 ("Find sums and differences of mixed tenths-and-hundredths numbers….") — students attempt all six parts, choosing their preferred method. Teacher collects responses to items (c) and (f) on the board to discuss regrouping across place values.

periods.teacher_notes: The structural-similarity observation — that 15 3/10 4/100 – 2 6/10 8/100 mirrors 653 – 268 column by column — is the conceptual payoff of section 3.3; make it explicit by writing both calculations side by side. A frequent error is aligning digits by count rather than by place value when tenths and hundredths appear in the same column; reinforce the alignment rule. The Math Talk item's two-method comparison is preparation for the decimal column form introduced in section 3.7.

periods.activity_title: Why Ten? Extending the Place Value Chain

textbook_items_in_class.description: Discuss: could 4 2/10 be written as 42 skipping the fraction denominator? What ambiguity arises? Show three different quantities that could all be denoted '705' without a positional separator.

How Big? Answer: (a) how many thousandths make one unit; (b) how many thousandths make one tenth; (c) how many thousandths make one hundredth; (d) how many tenths make one ten; (e) how many hundredths make one ten. Then make a few more similar questions and answer them.

Make a place value table (hundreds, tens, units, tenths, hundredths, thousandths). Write each quantity in decimal form, place value expansion, and read aloud: (a) 2 ones, 3 tenths, 5 hundredths; (b) 1 ten and 5 tenths; (c) 4 ones and 6 hundredths; (d) 1 hundred, 1 one and 1 hundredth; (e) 8/100 and 9/10; (f) 5/100; (g) 1/10; (h) 2 1/100, 4 1/10, 7 1/1000.
Write in decimal form: (a) 234 hundredths; (b) 105 tenths.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the deductive argument from section 3.4: the place value chain extends leftward (10,000 → 1,000 → 100 → 10 → 1) by dividing by 10 each step, so extending rightward follows the same rule (1 → 1/10 → 1/100 → 1/1000). Students trace the chain on paper and answer: why not split into 4 or 8 equal parts? Draw the answer from the base-ten structure.

Math Talk, section 3.4 p.61 ("Discuss: could 4 2/10 be written as 42….") — students reason in pairs about the ambiguity in the '705' string, then the decimal point is introduced as the positional separator that resolves the ambiguity. Teacher shows 705, 70.5, and 7.05 on the same place value table.

Figure it Out, section 3.4 p.61 ("How Big?….") and Figure it Out, section 3.4 p.63 ("Make a place value table….") — students complete the 'How Big?' items first to anchor the chain, then build the full place value table and write each of the eight quantities in decimal form, reading them aloud.

Figure it Out, section 3.4 p.64 ("Write in decimal form: 234 hundredths; 105 tenths.") — students apply place value decomposition to convert improper-fractional counts to decimal notation. Teacher confirms using the worked example (234 tenths = 23.4) from the section prose.

periods.teacher_notes: The deductive step — extending the place value chain rightward by the same ÷10 rule — is the conceptual hinge of section 3.4; hold students to articulating the reason before accepting a numerical answer. Students commonly misplace the decimal point in 234 hundredths, writing 23.4 instead of 2.34; the place value table catches this if students use it faithfully. The measurement conversions in section 3.5 are handled in the apply unit (unit 7), but note that the 'How Big?' item (E-16) builds the thousandths intuition needed there.
materials: Place value table templates (printed or drawn on paper)

periods.activity_title: Decimals in Measurement and on the Number Line

textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks for mm ↔ cm conversions: 70 mm = ___ cm; ___ = 0.9 cm; 134 mm = ___; ___ = 203.6 cm.
Fill in the blanks for cm ↔ m conversions: 36 cm = ___; 50 cm = ___; ___ = 0.89 m; 4 cm = ___; 325 cm = ___; ___ = 2.07 m. Then answer: how many mm in 1 m? Can 1 mm = 1/1000 m?
Draw a number line and locate 1.4 by dividing the unit between 1 and 2 into 10 equal parts. Name all the divisions between 1 and 1.1.
Zero Dilemma: Sonu says 0.2 = 0.20 = 0.200. Zara disagrees. Use the place value table to settle the dispute; then determine which of 4.5, 4.05, 0.405, 4.050, 4.50, 4.005, 04.50 are equal.

homework.description: Fill in the blanks for g ↔ kg conversions: 465 g = ___; 68 g = ___; 1560 g = ___; 704 g = ___; ___ = 0.56 kg; ___ = 2.5 kg.

time_bands.activity: Teacher derives the unit-fraction conversions from section 3.5 on the board: 1 mm = 0.1 cm, 1 cm = 0.01 m. Students apply these to Figure it Out, section 3.5 p.64 ("Fill in the blanks for mm ↔ cm conversions….") and Figure it Out, section 3.5 p.66 ("Fill in the blanks for cm ↔ m conversions….") independently, then confirm the thousandths connection (1 mm = 0.001 m).

Figure it Out, section 3.6 p.70 ("Draw a number line and locate 1.4….") — students draw the number line, divide the unit interval into 10 equal parts, and label each tenth division between 1 and 2. They name every subdivision between 1 and 1.1 using decimal notation, connecting place value to spatial position.

Math Talk, section 3.6 p.70 ("Zero Dilemma: Sonu says 0.2 = 0.20 = 0.200….") — pairs settle the dispute using the place value table, then determine which of the seven listed decimals are equal. Teacher confirms by plotting two or three on the number line to show that trailing zeros leave the point's position unchanged.

Quick close: teacher poses '6.456 vs. 6.465 — which is greater?' Students compare digit by digit from left to right and state the answer with one-sentence justification. Homework (g ↔ kg conversions, section 3.5 p.68) is set.

periods.teacher_notes: The measurement conversions and the number line are taught in one unit because both apply the decimal place value structure established in section 3.4; framing them together reinforces that decimal notation is a system, not a collection of rules. Watch for students who append zeros to change the decimal's value — the Zero Dilemma item is the direct antidote. For the cm ↔ m conversions, check that students derive the unit fraction (1 cm = 1/100 m = 0.01 m) rather than memorising a 'move the decimal point' rule.

periods.activity_title: Zooming In, Adding Up, and Real-World Decimals

textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify the decimal number denoted by '?' in figure (b), where successive zooms of the number line are given (similar to how 4.185 is located in figure (a)).
Write the detailed place value computation for 84.691 – 77.345 and its compact column form.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.7 p.75
Figure it Out Q1, section 3.8 p.78
textbook_items_in_class.description: Convert fractions into decimals: (a) 5/100; (b) 16/1000; (c) 12/10; (d) 254/1000.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.7 p.75

time_bands.activity: Figure it Out, section 3.6 p.71 ("Identify the decimal number denoted by '?'….") — teacher demonstrates successive-magnification reading using figure (a) (locating 4.185) on the board; students then read figure (b) independently, naming the three levels of zoom and writing the decimal at each stage.

Teacher connects the section 3.7 cloth-purchase context (2.7 m + 3.5 m) to the fraction form shown earlier, writing the column addition with decimal points aligned. Try This, section 3.7 p.75 ("Write the detailed place value computation for 84.691 – 77.345….") is attempted by students immediately after: expand, subtract column by column, then write compact form.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.7 p.75 ("Find the sums….") — students work all eight additions in column form, paying particular attention to (f) 0.934 + 0.6, where the addends have different numbers of decimal places. Teacher circulates and highlights the placeholder zero convention.

Figure it Out Q1, section 3.8 p.78 ("Convert fractions into decimals….") — students convert four fractions (denominators 10, 100, 1000) to decimal notation using the place value table. Teacher briefly introduces section 3.8's theme — real-world consequences of decimal errors — through the Air Canada and medical-dosing vignettes as a closing hook. Homework subtraction set is assigned.

periods.teacher_notes: Bringing sections 3.6, 3.7, and 3.8 into one unit ensures all registry sections are taught before the synthesis unit; the successive-magnification work from section 3.6 is a quick visual recall, and the fraction-to-decimal conversions from section 3.8 apply the place value chain already established. The most common column-addition error is misaligning decimal points when addends have different decimal lengths — use (f) 0.934 + 0.6 to show placeholder zeros explicitly. The Air Canada vignette is motivational context, not an assessed item; do not extend it past the brief hook.

Refer to Prepared Table (see material: 'Problems and solutions') for the problems in full and their worked solutions. Pose all four problems at once on the board. Students work individually in silence for the first stretch, writing full working in their exercise books. They then compare answers in groups of three; any disagreement is resolved by rebuilding the solution step by step, not by voting. One student per problem presents to the class, and after each presentation the class names the chapter method the solution depended on. Problem 1 calls on unit conversion using the decimal place value chain (section 3.5). Problem 2 calls on decimal column addition with regrouping (section 3.7). Problem 3 calls on left-to-right digit comparison to locate a decimal on the number line (section 3.6). Problem 4 calls on place value expansion to read and write a decimal in its component parts (section 3.4). Watch for: in Problem 1, students multiplying instead of dividing when converting mm to m; in Problem 2, misaligning decimal points in column addition; in Problem 3, students ranking by digit count rather than by place value; in Problem 4, students omitting a zero placeholder in the hundredths column.

visual_aids.title: Problems and solutions
visual_aids.table:
No. | Problem | Solution
1 | A ribbon measures 235 mm. Write its length in centimetres and in metres, using decimal notation. | 1 mm = 0.1 cm, so 235 mm = 235 × 0.1 cm = 23.5 cm. 1 cm = 0.01 m, so 23.5 cm = 23.5 × 0.01 m = 0.235 m. (Check: 1 mm = 0.001 m, so 235 mm = 0.235 m. ✓)
2 | Three pieces of wire have lengths 4.76 m, 0.8 m, and 12.09 m. What is their total length? | Align decimal points and add column by column. Thousandths: none. Hundredths: 6 + 0 + 9 = 15; write 5, carry 1. Tenths: 7 + 8 + 0 + 1 (carry) = 16; write 6, carry 1. Units: 4 + 0 + 2 + 1 (carry) = 7. Tens: 0 + 0 + 1 = 1. Total = 17.65 m.
3 | Four students read the same thermometer and write down: 36.8°, 36.08°, 36.80°, and 36.089°. Arrange the readings in increasing order and state which two are equal. | Compare left to right. All have 36 as the whole-number part. Tenths: 36.08 and 36.089 have tenths digit 0; 36.8 and 36.80 have tenths digit 8, so both of the first pair are smaller. Between 36.08 and 36.089: they agree up to the hundredths digit, and 36.089 carries a thousandths digit 9 against 0, so 36.08 < 36.089. Finally 36.80 = 36.8 — a trailing zero does not change the value. Order: 36.08 < 36.089 < 36.8 = 36.80. The two equal readings are 36.8 and 36.80.
4 | Write 0.407 in its full place value expansion (as a sum of tenths, hundredths, and thousandths), then write the decimal number whose place value expansion is 3 tenths + 0 hundredths + 6 thousandths. | 0.407 = 4/10 + 0/100 + 7/1000, i.e. 4 tenths, 0 hundredths, 7 thousandths. For the second part: 3 tenths + 0 hundredths + 6 thousandths = 0.306 (the 0 in the hundredths place must be written to hold position).

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes all four problems on the board, reads each aloud once, and confirms that every student has understood the question before anyone begins. No hints are given. Students open their exercise books to a fresh page.

Individual silent work. Every student attempts all four problems, writing complete working — not just answers — in their exercise book. Teacher circulates without correcting, noting which problems produce the most hesitation.

Groups of three compare answers. Where two students disagree with the third, the group rebuilds that solution from its first step. Teacher prompts any group that has stalled by asking which chapter idea the problem is using, without supplying the method itself.

One student presents each problem at the board, showing full working. After each presentation the class — not the teacher — names the chapter method the solution rested on (conversion using unit fractions; column addition with aligned decimal points; left-to-right place value comparison; place value expansion and the zero placeholder). The teacher confirms or corrects the naming.

Closing. The teacher states: every problem yielded because each digit in a decimal number carries a fixed value determined by its position in the base-ten place value chain — that single idea is what the chapter is about.

goals.anchor_description: Mahi buys 0.25 kg beans, 0.3 kg carrots, 0.5 kg potatoes, 0.2 kg capsicums, 0.05 kg ginger. Calculate total weight.

items.prompt: A student places a pencil on a millimetre-ruled scale. The pencil ends between the 12 cm and 13 cm marks, at the seventh small division past 12 cm. Which expression correctly records the pencil's length?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each small division between consecutive centimetre marks is one tenth of a centimetre, so seven divisions past 12 cm gives 12 7/10 cm.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses the size of a millimetre division with one hundredth of a centimetre, placing the digit in the wrong fractional position.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student concatenates the whole-centimetre reading and the tick count without inserting any fractional notation, treating the length as 127 whole centimetres.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student mis-groups the digits, reading '1 ten and 27 tenths' rather than '12 whole centimetres and 7 tenths'.

inclusivity.support: Let the student draw a 1 cm segment divided into 10 equal parts and count to the seventh tick.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to record the same length as an improper fraction in tenths and explain why both forms name the same point on the scale.

exercise.description: Measure the lengths of a pen, sharpener, and an object of the student's choice using a scale; record the measurements in centimetres using tenth notation as modelled in the section.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly expresses the length 27 one-tenths as a mixed number?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 27 tenths by 10: 27 ÷ 10 = 2 remainder 7, giving 2 whole units and 7/10.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student takes the digit '2' as tens rather than as the whole-unit count, failing to complete the division.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student changes the denominator to 100 without any regrouping, confusing tenths with hundredths.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student writes 70/10 for the fractional part instead of 7/10, multiplying the remainder by 10 erroneously.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to refer back to the pencil-length diagram in section 3.2 that shows 34 one-tenths = 3 4/10.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write 27/10 as a decimal and explain which digit sits in the tenths place.

exercise.description: Write lengths of objects (USB cable, and others shown in diagrams) in two ways — as a mixed number and as an improper tenth fraction — and read them aloud.

items.prompt: How many one-hundredths are equal to 3/10?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each one-tenth contains 10 one-hundredths, so 3 tenths = 3 × 10 = 30 hundredths.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses tenths and hundredths as if they were the same unit, reading the numerator directly.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student multiplies by 100 instead of 10, not recognising that only one step separates tenths from hundredths.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student inverts the relationship, thinking of hundredths as smaller than tenths by a factor of 3 rather than 10.

inclusivity.support: Let the student sketch a unit strip divided into 10 tenths, then shade 3 and subdivide those into 10 parts each to count.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to express 3/10 in three equivalent forms: as a fraction with denominator 100, as a mixed tenths-and-hundredths expression, and in decimal notation.

exercise.description: How many one-hundredths make one-tenth? Can the folded-paper length also be stated as 4 units and 45 one-hundredths? Explain.

items.prompt: The digit string '305' could mean three hundred and five, or thirty and five-tenths, or three and five-hundredths. Explain, in two or three sentences, why the decimal point is necessary to remove this ambiguity. In your answer, state what each place in the decimal number 30.5 represents.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Without a positional separator, the same digit string 305 could represent whole numbers or mixed quantities at different scales — there is no way to tell which digit occupies which place. The decimal point fixes the units position: in 30.5, the digit 3 is in the tens place (value 30), the digit 0 is in the units place (value 0), and the digit 5 is in the tenths place (value 5/10 = 0.5). The decimal point thus extends the base-ten place value chain rightward to fractional values, making every digit's meaning unambiguous.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the place value chain (tens → units → tenths) and show that each digit's value depends on its position relative to the decimal point.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to talk through the answer with a partner before writing, using the place value table drawn in class.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to alter one premise: if instead we used a comma separator (as in some European countries), would the same ambiguity problem arise? Why or why not?

exercise.description: Discuss: could 4 2/10 be written as 42 skipping the fraction denominator? What ambiguity arises? Show three different quantities that could all be denoted '705' without a positional separator.

items.prompt: A ribbon is cut into three pieces. The first piece is 3 4/10 units long, the second is 2 8/10 units long, and the third is 1 5/10 units long. What is the total length of ribbon used? Show your working using the 'units and tenths separately' method.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add whole units and tenths separately; regroup 17 tenths as 1 unit 7 tenths and combine with the whole-unit sum.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student draw three strips on a number line and combine them, trading 10 tenths for 1 unit when the tenths total exceeds 9.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to verify the answer by also using the 'convert all to tenths' method and confirm both methods give the same result.

exercise.description: Find the total length of a honeybee given head = 2 3/10 units, thorax = 5 4/10 units, abdomen = 7 5/10 units.

items.prompt: From a wire of length 8 3/10 5/100 units, a piece of 3 7/10 9/100 units is cut off. What length of wire remains? Show column-wise working, treating tenths and hundredths as separate columns.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Hundredths column: 5 – 9 requires borrowing; borrow 1 tenth → tenths become 2/10 and hundredths become 15/100. 15 – 9 = 6 hundredths. Tenths column: 2 – 7 requires borrowing; borrow 1 unit → units become 7, tenths become 12/10. 12 – 7 = 5 tenths. Units column: 7 – 3 = 4 units. Remaining length = 4 5/10 6/100 units.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply column subtraction with regrouping across the hundredths, tenths, and units columns in order.

inclusivity.support: Suggest converting both lengths to hundredths first (835/100 – 379/100) as an alternate route to verify.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain why the regrouping steps here are structurally identical to subtracting 835 – 379 in whole-number arithmetic.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.55
exercise.description: In seven groups (a)–(g), identify the longest and shortest length from the given set of tenths and hundredths values, and mark each length on the scale: (a) 3/10, 3/100, 33/100; (b) 3 1/10, 30/10, 1 3/10; (c) 45/100, 54/100, 5/10, 4/10; (d) 3 6/10, 3 6/100, 3 6/10 6/100; (e) 8 2/100, 9/100, 1 8/100; (f) 7 3/10 5/100, 7 5/10, 7 41/100; (g) 65/10 15/100, 5 87/100, 5 7/100.

items.prompt: A packet of flour weighs 1250 g. Express this weight in kilograms as a decimal. Then express it in decimal notation using the unit fraction 1 g = 0.001 kg.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1 g = 0.001 kg, so 1250 g = 1250 × 0.001 kg = 1.250 kg, which equals 1.25 kg. The trailing zero does not change the value, so the weight is 1.25 kg.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the unit fraction 1 g = 1/1000 kg = 0.001 kg; multiply by 1250, then simplify trailing zeros.

inclusivity.support: Suggest starting from the known fact 1000 g = 1 kg and dividing both sides: 1250 g = 1000 g + 250 g = 1 kg + 250/1000 kg.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to also express 1250 g in decimal form in milligrams and in tonnes, deriving each unit fraction from the chain 1 mg = 0.001 g = 0.000001 kg.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks for mm ↔ cm conversions: 70 mm = ___ cm; ___ = 0.9 cm; 134 mm = ___; ___ = 203.6 cm.

items.prompt: Three decimal numbers — 3.07, 3.70, and 3.7 — are to be placed on a number line between 3 and 4. Without drawing, explain which of the three is greatest, which is least, and which two are equal. Justify using digit-by-digit comparison.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: All three have the same units digit 3. Compare tenths: 3.07 has 0 in the tenths place while 3.70 and 3.7 have 7 in the tenths place, so 3.07 is the least. For 3.70 vs 3.7: the trailing zero in 3.70 does not add value (the hundredths digit is 0), so 3.70 = 3.7. Therefore 3.70 and 3.7 are equal and greatest; 3.07 is the least.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare digit by digit from left to right, and apply the trailing-zero rule to confirm 3.70 = 3.7.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to write each number in a place value table (units | tenths | hundredths) before comparing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if a fourth number 3.700 is introduced, where does it sit? Change one digit in 3.07 to make it fall exactly between 3.7 and 3.8.

exercise.description: Draw a number line and locate 1.4 by dividing the unit between 1 and 2 into 10 equal parts. Name all the divisions between 1 and 1.1.

items.prompt: A shopkeeper has 14.75 m of cloth. She sells 6.8 m in the morning and 3.45 m in the afternoon. How many metres of cloth remain? Show column working with decimal points aligned.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total sold = 6.8 + 3.45. Align: 6.80 + 3.45 = 10.25 m. Remaining = 14.75 – 10.25. Align: 14.75 – 10.25 = 4.50 m, which equals 4.5 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the two sold quantities using column addition with placeholder zero, then subtract from the original stock using column subtraction.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student use a number line to perform 14.75 – 6.8 first, then subtract 3.45 from the result as two separate steps.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to verify: does the answer lie strictly between 14 – 10 = 4 and 15 – 10 = 5? Apply Sonu's sum-range reasoning to the intermediate addition 6.8 + 3.45 as a check.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.7 p.75

items.prompt: A nurse must administer 0.125 mg of a medicine but misreads the decimal and gives 1.25 mg instead. By how much does the actual dose exceed the correct dose? Express your answer as a decimal in milligrams and explain in one sentence why this kind of error is dangerous.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Excess dose = 1.25 – 0.125. Align: 1.250 – 0.125 = 1.125 mg. The actual dose is 10 times the intended dose, which is dangerous because a dose ten times larger than prescribed can cause serious harm or be fatal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract using column form with placeholder zero (1.250 – 0.125 = 1.125), then interpret the scale of the error in context.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student first compare 1.25 and 0.125 on a place value table to confirm which is larger, then set up the column subtraction.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the correct dose is 0.125 mg and the error is a factor of 10, what decimal would represent a dose 100 times too large? Express it and compute the excess.
